nodes.label: Thermodynamics
nodes.note: Thermodynamics links heat, work, and internal energy, with calorimetry and change of state as its working tools. The core accounting identity is the first law: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$.

nodes.label: Heat and Calorimetry
nodes.note: Heat is energy in transit; calorimetry measures it. The working relation is $$Q = mc\Delta T$$ for a temperature change without phase change.

nodes.label: Mechanical Equivalent of Heat
nodes.note: Joule's paddle-wheel experiment fixed the conversion between work and heat: $$W = JQ, \ J = 4.2\ \text{J}/\text{cal}$$. It unified mechanical and thermal energy.

nodes.label: Specific Heat Capacity
nodes.note: Heat needed to raise unit mass by one degree: $$Q = mc\Delta T$$. Water's high specific heat $c = 4186\ \text{J}/\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}$ makes it a thermal buffer in nature and exam tricks.

nodes.label: Thermal Capacity and Molar Heat
nodes.note: Thermal capacity of a body is $C = mc$, and molar heat capacity is $$C_m = \frac{Q}{n\Delta T}$$. The solid-liquid distinction appears when comparing $C_V$ and $C_P$ for gases.

nodes.label: Principle of Calorimetry
nodes.note: In an isolated system the heat lost by hot bodies equals heat gained by cold bodies: $$\sum Q_{\text{lost}} = \sum Q_{\text{gained}}$$. Mixing problems are solved by this single balance equation.

nodes.label: Water Equivalent of Calorimeter
nodes.note: A calorimeter absorbs heat like an equivalent mass of water: $$(m_1c_1 + W)\Delta T_1 = m_2c_2\Delta T_2$$. Omitting water equivalent is the most common JEE calorimetry error.

nodes.label: Calorimetry Mixing Algorithm
nodes.note: For a hot body in cold water: $$m_h c_h (T_h - T_f) = m_c c_c (T_f - T_c)$$. Solve iteratively when ice is present by first checking whether all ice melts.

nodes.label: Ice-Water Mixture Check
nodes.note: Before mixing, compare heat needed to melt all ice, $$Q_{melt} = m_{ice}L_f$$, with heat available from cooling water. The comparison decides whether the final state is all-liquid or a mixture at $0^\circ\text{C}$.

nodes.label: Change of State
nodes.note: Phase changes absorb latent heat at constant temperature: $$Q = mL$$, where $L$ is the latent heat of fusion or vaporisation.

nodes.label: Latent Heat
nodes.note: Latent heat of fusion for ice is about $3.34 \times 10^5\ \text{J}/\text{kg}$: $$Q = mL_f$$. During $L_f$ transfer the temperature stays pinned at $0^\circ\text{C}$.

nodes.label: Heating Curve Analysis
nodes.note: On a temperature vs heat graph, sloped parts follow $Q = mc\Delta T$ and flat plateaus follow $Q = mL$. The slope inverts between solid, liquid, and gas because the $c$ values differ.

nodes.label: Regelation and Melting Point
nodes.note: Pressure lowers the melting point of ice (anomalous), enabling regelation: $$\frac{dT}{dP} = \frac{T(V_l - V_s)}{L}$$. The negative sign of $V_l - V_s$ for ice is the entire physics.

nodes.label: Sublimation
nodes.note: Solids passing directly to vapour absorb latent heat of sublimation: $$Q = mL_s, \ L_s = L_f + L_v$$. Dry ice and camphor are textbook cases.

nodes.label: Triple Point of Water
nodes.note: The unique $(T, P)$ where solid, liquid, and vapour coexist: $$T = 273.16\ \text{K}, \ P = 611.657\ \text{Pa}$$. It defines the kelvin.

nodes.label: Thermal Expansion
nodes.note: Solids, liquids, and gases expand on heating; linear expansion is $$\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$$.

nodes.label: Linear Expansion
nodes.note: Fractional length change is linear in temperature: $$\frac{\Delta L}{L_0} = \alpha \Delta T$$. The coefficient $\alpha$ differs by material and sets bimetallic behavior.

nodes.label: Superficial and Volumetric Expansion
nodes.note: For isotropic solids, area and volume coefficients relate as $$\beta \approx 2\alpha, \ \gamma \approx 3\alpha$$. Liquids are quoted by $\gamma$ since only volume matters.

nodes.label: Bimetallic Strip
nodes.note: Two bonded strips bend toward the lower-$\alpha$ side on heating: $$\Delta L_{rel} = (\alpha_2 - \alpha_1)L_0\Delta T$$. This differential expansion drives thermostat switches.

nodes.label: Thermal Stress in Clamped Rods
nodes.note: A rod prevented from expanding develops compressive stress: $$\sigma = Y\alpha\Delta T$$, with force $F = YA\alpha\Delta T$. It is why bridges have expansion joints.

nodes.label: Anomalous Expansion of Water
nodes.note: Water contracts from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $4^\circ\text{C}$ and is densest at $4^\circ\text{C}$. Density variation follows $$\rho(T) \approx \rho_0[1 - \gamma (T - 4)]$$ in that window.

nodes.label: Real vs Apparent Expansion of Liquids
nodes.note: A liquid in a vessel expands apparently because the vessel expands too: $$\gamma_{real} = \gamma_{app} + \gamma_{vessel}$$. Overflow method problems use exactly this bookkeeping.

nodes.label: Density Variation with Temperature
nodes.note: $$\rho_T = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} \approx \rho_0(1 - \gamma \Delta T)$$. Mass is conserved during thermal expansion, so density falls.

nodes.label: Laws of Thermodynamics
nodes.note: The laws define temperature, constrain energy conversion, and forbid perfect engines. The first law is an energy ledger: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$.

nodes.label: Zeroth Law and Temperature
nodes.note: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and C are at equal temperature: symmetry and transitivity of equilibrium. Temperature is the only state function this defines.

nodes.label: First Law of Thermodynamics
nodes.note: $$\Delta U = Q - W$$, with $W$ the work done by the gas and $\Delta U$ depending only on endpoints: $$W = \int P\,dV$$. Sign conventions flip $W$ in chemistry texts.

nodes.label: Internal Energy of an Ideal Gas
nodes.note: Internal energy is kinetic only, hence temperature-only for an ideal gas: $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$$. This is why isothermal ideal-gas processes have $\Delta U = 0$.

nodes.label: Second Law Statements
nodes.note: Kelvin-Planck: no engine converts heat from a single reservoir fully into work. Clausius: heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot. Both imply entropy increases: $$\Delta S_{univ} \ge 0$$.

nodes.label: Thermodynamic Processes
nodes.note: Each canonical process pins one variable or constraint, simplifying the first law. For a polytropic change $$PV^x = \text{constant}$$.

nodes.label: Isochoric Process
nodes.note: Constant volume gives $W = 0$, so all heat changes internal energy: $$Q = \Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$$. On a P-V diagram it is a vertical line.

nodes.label: Isobaric Process
nodes.note: At constant pressure, work is $$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$$ and heat absorbed is $$Q = nC_P\Delta T$$. The gap $C_P - C_V = R$ measures expansion work.

nodes.label: Isothermal Process
nodes.note: For an ideal gas at constant $T$, $\Delta U = 0$ and $$W = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$. The P-V curve is a rectangular hyperbola $PV = $ const.

nodes.label: Adiabatic Process
nodes.note: With $Q = 0$, the gas obeys $$PV^\gamma = \text{constant}, \ T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{constant}$$ and $W = \frac{P_1V_1 - P_2V_2}{\gamma - 1}$. Compression heats the gas rapidly.

nodes.label: Free Expansion
nodes.note: An ideal gas expanding into vacuum does no work and exchanges no heat, so $$\Delta U = 0, \ \Delta T = 0$$. Entropy still rises: $$\Delta S = nR\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$.

nodes.label: Work on P-V, V-T, P-T Diagrams
nodes.note: Work equals the enclosed area in a cyclic process: $$W_{cycle} = \oint P\,dV$$. Clockwise cycles output positive net work.

nodes.label: Role of Gamma in Adiabatics
nodes.note: Steeper adiabats on a P-V plot follow $$P \propto V^{-\gamma}$$ with $\gamma > 1$. The isotherm is $PV = \text{const}$, noticeably flatter.

nodes.label: Heat Engines and Entropy
nodes.note: Engines convert heat between reservoirs with bounded efficiency. Carnot sets the ceiling: $$\eta_{max} = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$.

nodes.label: Heat Engine Efficiency
nodes.note: Efficiency is work output over heat input: $$\eta = \frac{W}{Q_1} = 1 - \frac{Q_2}{Q_1}$$. Real engines underperform Carnot because of friction and finite-rate heat flow.

nodes.label: Carnot Cycle
nodes.note: Two isotherms and two adiabatics give the reversible benchmark: $$\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$$. Kelvin temperatures must be used, so $T_2 < T_1$ always.

nodes.label: Entropy and Clausius Inequality
nodes.note: Entropy change for a reversible path is $$\Delta S = \int \frac{dQ_{rev}}{T}$$, and for any cycle $$\oint \frac{dQ}{T} \le 0$$. Free expansion of a gas creates entropy with no heat transfer at all.

nodes.label: Refrigerator and Heat Pump
nodes.note: A reversed engine moves heat from cold to hot using work: $$K_{fridge} = \frac{Q_2}{W} = \frac{T_2}{T_1 - T_2}$$. Heat pump COP exceeds 1 because it delivers $Q_1 = Q_2 + W$.

nodes.label: Heat Transfer
nodes.note: Heat moves by conduction, convection, and radiation. Conduction through a slab follows Fourier's law: $$\frac{dQ}{dt} = -kA\frac{dT}{dx}$$.

nodes.label: Conduction and Thermal Resistance
nodes.note: In series, resistances add; in parallel, conductances add: $$R_{th} = \frac{x}{kA}, \ R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2$$. Composite-wall JEE problems are resistor problems in disguise.

nodes.label: Newton's Law of Cooling
nodes.note: Cooling rate is proportional to the excess temperature: $$\frac{dT}{dt} = -k(T - T_0)$$. Integrating gives exponential approach to ambient.

nodes.label: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiation
nodes.note: Radiated power scales as the fourth power of absolute temperature: $$P = \sigma e A T^4, \ \sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{W}/\text{m}^2\text{K}^4$$. Net exchange uses $T^4 - T_0^4$.
